intro.heading: The drill is done. Now you need to know it landed.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care homes.
intro.paragraph: The alarm sounded at two in the afternoon and the day team met at the assembly point in good time. The manager thanked everyone, filled in the drill form and went back to the office. A week later a new carer, who started the day before the drill, is asked where the nearest fire door is on her corridor and hesitates. The manager realises the form shows when the drill happened and who took part. It does not show who understood what to do, or who was too busy dealing with the alarm to take it in.

trail.text: The alarm sounds and the day team reaches the assembly point.
The manager thanks everyone and runs a quick talk in the corridor.
The drill form is filled in and filed.
Nobody has checked what anyone remembers of the talk.
A carer who started the day before and followed others out.
A carer who was in a resident's room and only heard part of the briefing.
A form showing a drill took place. Nothing showing what was understood.
“What would you do if the alarm sounded now?” A form cannot answer for them.

trail_close: The drill was real work and it counted. What is missing is a quick, kind way to check what stuck, and a short lesson for anything that did not.

why.heading: A drill record shows what happened, not what was understood
why.sub: Staff can take part in a drill and still not know the next step on their own.

cards.title: Following the crowd is not knowing
cards.body: In a drill many carers walk out with the group. That is fine on the day, but it does not show they could act alone, or cover a different part of the building.

cards.title: New and part time staff see less
cards.body: People on different shifts, new starters and agency staff may miss the briefing. Nobody notices until someone is asked a direct question.

cards.title: Memory fades without a prompt
cards.body: A short talk in a corridor is easy to forget. A quick check a week later is a fair way to see what has stayed and what needs another look.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Does CareStream keep my fire drill record?
items.a: No. Keep your drill record as you do now. It shows the drill happened. CareStream adds a separate check on what staff understood afterwards, so you have both.

items.q: How do I check what staff remember after a drill?
items.a: A week or so later you allocate the Fire Safety module in the Training screen. It is a short quiz built from your own policies where they cover the topic. Staff complete it in the Staff Hub on their own phone.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into their Follow-up tab and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: Does it tell me every time someone slips?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the picture in Analytics, Knowledge gaps, and in a Monday digest email.

items.q: Is the lesson generic, or about how we work?
items.a: It uses your own policies where they cover the topic. Where they do not, it falls back on general good practice, which is a useful hint that the policy needs a look. Check your fire procedures are in place first.
Yes. You can edit and preview the module before you allocate it, so the questions fit your building and your fire procedures.

items.q: Does this replace the drill or the fire training?
items.a: No. Drills and practical fire training stay as they are. This checks understanding afterwards. It does not teach anyone how to use equipment or lead an evacuation.

items.q: What does it cost and can I try it?
items.a: There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans, and you can create a free account to look around. The adhoc training screen is on the paid plans, and you can see the plans on the pricing page.

faqs.heading: Fire safety checks and CareStream, answered

items.q: What is a good fire safety quiz for care home staff?
items.a: A short one, with three to five questions on what a carer would actually do. Ask about the first action, fire doors, the assembly point and how to raise the alarm. CareStream builds one from your own policies, and you can edit it first.

items.q: Is a quiz the same as fire safety awareness training?
items.a: No. Fire safety awareness training teaches the topic, and our Fire Safety course is one way to do that. A quiz afterwards checks what stuck.
A knowledge check is a few questions asked after training to see what someone remembers. In CareStream, a wrong answer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.

items.q: How soon after the drill should I send it?
items.a: About a week later is a sensible rule: late enough to show what stuck. You choose when to allocate it and can set a due date.

items.q: Does a fire drill record show staff understood?
items.a: It shows the drill took place. A quick check for understanding afterwards adds the other half, which is what people remembered. CareStream does not keep drill records.

items.q: Who is responsible for fire safety in a care home?
items.a: Under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, this sits with the responsible person, which is the employer for a workplace under their control. Your fire risk assessment should say who that is for your home.

items.q: Must employees be given fire safety training?
items.a: The same Order says the responsible person must ensure that employees are given adequate safety training, when they start and again where appropriate. A short quiz is one way to see how well it is landing.
No. Refresher training stays as you plan it. A quiz after a drill is a small extra check between refreshers, so you can see who needs another look.

guide.heading: A practical way to check understanding after a fire drill
guide.lede: A drill ends when the last person is back inside and the form is filed. What a manager really wants to know comes later: who could do it again, alone, without following the crowd.

sections.h3: Keep the check short and about real actions
paragraphs: Three to five questions is enough. Ask what a carer would do, not what a document says. Cover the first action on finding a fire, why fire doors stay closed, where to go and who to tell. Your own fire procedures decide the right answers, so write or edit the questions to match them.
Keep the tone kind. A wrong answer is information about where the next briefing needs to be clearer. It is not a mark against the carer.

sections.h3: Four checks that fit a busy home
checklist: Same day: a short talk after the drill, and your drill record filled in.
Within a week: allocate the Fire Safety module so each carer answers a few questions alone.
Whenever an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each month: look at the most missed questions and use them in the next drill briefing.

paragraphs: The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 puts duties on the responsible person, and article 21 covers training for employees. Check who that is for your home and keep your fire risk assessment close to hand.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the drill record, the quiz questions and the results together, so you can show understanding as well as that the drill took place.
